title: So What
description: The opening track of Kind of Blue — the best-selling jazz album of all time — caught here in a rare 1959 TV performance by Miles and his legendary sextet.

pops.text: Recorded March 2, 1959, at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in New York — a converted church musicians nicknamed 'The Church.'
Miles barely rehearsed the band. He handed the musicians scales and sketches instead of finished charts, then let the tape roll.
That's Bill Evans on piano and Paul Chambers on bass trading the famous call-and-response intro.
The whole tune is built on just two chords. Welcome to modal jazz — Miles wanted freedom, not chord changes.
John Coltrane takes the first tenor solo. Within a year he'd leave to form his own quartet and change jazz all over again.
Most of Kind of Blue was captured in first takes — Miles liked the sound of musicians thinking on their feet.
Jimmy Cobb's feather-light drumming keeps the whole thing floating. He was the last surviving member of this band, passing in 2020.
This footage comes from a CBS TV special filmed just weeks after the album session — some of the only video of this band in action.
Kind of Blue went on to become the best-selling jazz album of all time. Not bad for two days of work.
Rolling Stone ranked the album #12 on its 2003 list of the 500 greatest albums ever made.

title: Freddie Freeloader
description: A laid-back 12-bar blues from Kind of Blue — and the one track on the album where Wynton Kelly, not Bill Evans, sits at the piano.

pops.text: Same magical day as 'So What': March 2, 1959 — same band, same studio, same session.
Spot the difference: this is the only Kind of Blue track with Wynton Kelly on piano instead of Bill Evans.
Kelly was the blues specialist in Miles's band — and this tune is a pure, swinging 12-bar blues.
Miles named it for Freddie, a Philadelphia character famous for trying to cadge free drinks. A freeloader, indeed.
Just when the blues pattern feels settled, the final two bars of each chorus sneak in a surprise chord twist.
Miles takes the first solo — cool, economical, every note placed like he has all the time in the world.
Coltrane answers on tenor, already stretching toward the 'sheets of sound' he'd become famous for.
Producers Teo Macero and Irving Townsend mostly kept the tape rolling and stayed out of the way. Smart men.
Kind of Blue took just two sessions to record, with almost everything done in a single take.
The album has never gone out of print since 1959 — somebody new discovers this record every single day.

title: Take Five
description: Paul Desmond's 5/4 masterpiece from Time Out — the experimental odd-meter tune that accidentally became the best-known jazz single on Earth.

pops.text: First surprise: Dave Brubeck didn't write it. Alto saxophonist Paul Desmond — the man playing the melody — did.
Count it out: one-two-three, one-two. The tune swings in 5/4, a beat pop audiences weren't supposed to like.
Drummer Joe Morello wanted a tune in 5/4 to practice with. Desmond went home and wrote him one.
Time Out was an experiment — every track in an odd meter like 5/4 or 9/8. Columbia Records worried it might flop.
Instead, 'Take Five' climbed to #25 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1961 — radical time signature and all.
Desmond later admitted he thought of it as a minor piece — basically an excuse for a Joe Morello drum feature.
Brubeck's piano vamp never changes — he loops the same groove while Desmond floats on top.
Time Out became the first jazz album ever certified platinum in the United States.
When Desmond died in 1977, he left his 'Take Five' royalties to the American Red Cross — reportedly around $100,000 a year.
Brubeck made the cover of Time magazine in 1954 — only the second jazz musician ever to do so, after Louis Armstrong.

title: Blue Rondo à la Turk
description: The Time Out opener: a Turkish street rhythm in 9/8 that slams headlong into good old American swing — with a wink at Mozart in the title.

pops.text: The title riffs on Mozart — his famous 'Rondo alla Turca' — with a splash of jazz-blue on top.
Brubeck first heard this rhythm from street musicians in Turkey while touring Eurasia for the US State Department in 1958.
Count the beat: 2+2+2+3. Nine beats per bar, chopped Turkish-style — an aksak rhythm, which literally means 'limping.'
Brubeck came home from that 1958 tour with a notebook full of odd meters. Time Out was the result.
Mid-tune, everything relaxes into straight 4/4 swing for the solos — two musical worlds inside one track.
Listen closely to Paul Desmond's alto solo: that's a genuine cracked note in there — and they kept the take.
Time Out's abstract cover painting is by S. Neil Fujita, Columbia Records' star designer of the era.
Columbia's bosses feared an album of weird time signatures would tank. It became a jazz landmark instead.
Brubeck doubled down with a follow-up in even stranger meters — Time Further Out, in 1961.
Bassist Eugene Wright and drummer Joe Morello hold down a rhythm most bands would trip over.

title: 'Round Midnight
description: Monk's haunting signature tune — the most recorded jazz standard ever written by a jazz musician — performed live in Norway in 1966.

pops.text: Monk wrote this melody around 1940, years before the world knew his name.
Cootie Williams recorded it first in 1944; Monk's own first recording came in 1947 for Blue Note.
It went on to become the most recorded jazz standard composed by a jazz musician. Everybody plays this one.
That famous opening flourish? Dizzy Gillespie's 1940s arrangement added it — and it's been standard ever since.
This performance was filmed in Oslo, Norway, in 1966 — Monk's quartet, with Charlie Rouse on tenor sax.
That's Larry Gales on bass and Ben Riley on drums, Monk's road-tested rhythm team of the mid-'60s.
Monk's spiky, spacious piano style — full of surprise dissonances — earned him the nickname 'the High Priest of Bebop.'
Mid-solo, Monk might stop playing and dance around the piano while the band kept going. Genius had its own choreography.
Bernie Hanighen later added lyrics, but the melody never needed them. It's pure atmosphere.
Miles Davis, Ella Fitzgerald, Wes Montgomery — the cover versions of this one could fill a record store.

title: Straight, No Chaser
description: A 12-bar blues with a Monk twist: the theme keeps slipping sideways against the beat. First recorded at his 1951 Blue Note session.

pops.text: Yes, the title is a bar order — a shot served neat, with nothing to wash it down. The tune goes down just as strong.
Underneath all the angles, this is a straight 12-bar blues in B-flat. Monk just refuses to phrase it politely.
The melody keeps landing slightly sideways — Monk displaces the riff a little further each time through.
Monk first recorded this on July 23, 1951, for Blue Note Records, with Art Blakey driving the drums.
Also in that 1951 band: a young Milt Jackson on vibes, a few years before he co-founded the Modern Jazz Quartet.
Miles Davis loved this tune — he cut a famous version on his 1958 album Milestones, with Coltrane and Cannonball aboard.
Monk's trick here: repeat one short phrase but start it in a different place every chorus. Simple idea, endlessly sneaky.
Critics in the '40s called Monk's playing 'wrong.' Bebop's inner circle — Dizzy, Bird, Bud Powell — knew better.
Monk kept re-recording it across his career, even with a big band — the tune never stopped shape-shifting.
By 1964, the 'wrong-note' pianist was on the cover of Time magazine. Vindication tastes sweet.

title: The Girl from Ipanema
description: Bossa nova's defining moment: Jobim's ode to a girl walking to the beach in Rio, sung in Portuguese by João Gilberto and in English by his wife Astrud — who had never sung professionally before.

pops.text: She was real: teenager Heloísa Pinheiro, who walked past the songwriters' Rio bar every day on her way to the beach.
Antônio Carlos Jobim wrote the music; poet Vinícius de Moraes wrote the Portuguese words in 1962.
João Gilberto sings the first verse in Portuguese — his soft, behind-the-beat style basically invented bossa nova singing.
Then the twist: João's wife Astrud sings the English verse. She had never sung professionally in her life.
Astrud was only in the studio to watch her husband record — she got the job partly because she spoke English.
Recorded in March 1963 in New York for the album Getz/Gilberto, with Stan Getz's saxophone floating over everything.
The US hit single trimmed João's Portuguese verse so radio could start with Astrud's famous English vocal.
It hit #5 on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped the adult contemporary chart in 1964.
At the 1965 Grammys it won Record of the Year — and Getz/Gilberto became the first jazz album to win Album of the Year.
It's now one of the most recorded songs in history — hundreds of versions, from Frank Sinatra to Amy Winehouse.

title: Desafinado
description: The record that lit the bossa nova fuse in America: Getz's cool tenor and Charlie Byrd's nylon-string guitar, cut in a Washington DC church hall in a single afternoon.

pops.text: 'Desafinado' means 'slightly out of tune' in Portuguese — Jobim's wink at critics who claimed bossa nova singers couldn't sing in tune.
Jobim and Newton Mendonça wrote it in 1958 as a gentle tease aimed at amateur bossa singers who drifted off pitch.
Guitarist Charlie Byrd brought bossa nova records home from a State Department tour of South America and pitched the sound to Getz.
They recorded the album Jazz Samba in under two hours — in a church hall in Washington, DC, chosen for its lovely acoustics.
Only one song at the session needed a second take. Bossa nova, apparently, really is as relaxed as it sounds.
Jazz Samba shot to #1 on the Billboard album chart and kicked off America's early-'60s bossa nova craze.
The hit single was edited down to about a third of this full album version — you're hearing the whole, unhurried thing.
'Desafinado' earned Stan Getz the Grammy for Best Jazz Performance.
Within a year, everyone from Ella Fitzgerald to Elvis Presley was cutting bossa nova records.
Byrd played it all on an unamplified classical guitar — no amp, no effects, just fingers on nylon strings.

title: Don't Know Why
description: The hushed breakthrough single from Come Away with Me — a Jesse Harris song that turned a 22-year-old jazz singer into a Grammy-sweeping phenomenon.

pops.text: Norah didn't write this one — her friend and guitarist Jesse Harris did. He'd recorded it himself back in 1999.
Harris is right there in the band, playing guitar behind his own song.
Norah is the daughter of sitar legend Ravi Shankar — though she grew up in Texas with her mom, concert producer Sue Jones.
Before this, she was singing in New York clubs and working restaurant shifts while Blue Note — a jazz label — took a chance on her.
Legendary producer Arif Mardin, who'd worked with Aretha Franklin and Dusty Springfield, kept the arrangement whisper-quiet.
Come Away with Me was recorded partly at Allaire Studios, a converted mansion in the Catskills in upstate New York.
At the 2003 Grammys this won Record of the Year and Song of the Year — the songwriting trophy went to Jesse Harris.
Norah also won Best Female Pop Vocal Performance for it. The album collected eight Grammys in all.
She was just 22 when the album came out — and famously shy about the avalanche of fame that followed.
The single itself only peaked at #30 on the Hot 100. It just never went away — there's a difference.

title: Come Away with Me
description: Norah's own title track — a moonlit invitation shot as a lone drive through the California desert, from the best-selling debut album of its era.

pops.text: This one Norah wrote herself, words and music — unlike her Harris-penned hit 'Don't Know Why.'
The video, directed by James Frost, is just Norah, an old car, and an endless desert highway.
It was filmed out in the California desert — all that golden emptiness is the real Mojave, no green screen.
Released in September 2002, it was the album's third single — the slow-burn favorite that kept the record climbing.
Come Away with Me the album eventually sold more than 25 million copies worldwide. For a quiet little jazz record!
It earned a rare Diamond certification in the US — ten million copies in America alone.
The song also turns up on the Maid in Manhattan soundtrack — it became the unofficial sound of early-2000s romance.
Producer Arif Mardin recorded the band live in the room, vocals and all — that's why it sounds like she's singing in your living room.
Before fame, Norah studied jazz piano at the University of North Texas, then left for New York to find her sound.
Two decades on, this remains one of the best-selling albums of the 21st century.

title: The Look of Love
description: Krall's lush, after-midnight take on the Bacharach–David classic, wrapped in Claus Ogerman's orchestrations and the strings of the London Symphony Orchestra.

pops.text: Burt Bacharach and Hal David wrote this in 1967 for Dusty Springfield — it debuted in the James Bond spoof Casino Royale.
Dusty Springfield's original version earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song.
Arranger Claus Ogerman was a legend himself — he'd crafted the classic Sinatra–Jobim albums a generation earlier.
Those strings are the London Symphony Orchestra — Krall cut her sixth album with full orchestral backing.
The Look of Love album became Krall's first platinum-selling record in the United States.
Krall grew up in Nanaimo, British Columbia — and was playing piano in local restaurants and bars by age 15.
Her mentor was bassist Ray Brown, Oscar Peterson's legendary bassist, who pushed the piano prodigy to sing as well as play.
Longtime producer Tommy LiPuma keeps her voice close-miked and right in your ear — very late-night, very last-drink.
The glamorous video goes full old-Hollywood — fitting, since the whole album plays like a movie for your ears.
Krall has won five Grammy Awards, and nine of her albums have debuted at #1 on the Billboard jazz chart.

title: 'Deed I Do
description: A finger-snapping 1926 standard swung Krall's way — from her Nat King Cole Trio tribute album All for You, seen here in her Live in Paris concert performance.

pops.text: This standard dates to 1926, written by Fred Rose and Walter Hirsch — a hit back in the flapper era.
Krall's version comes from All for You (1996), her loving tribute to the Nat King Cole Trio.
Like Cole's trio, her tribute band is piano, guitar and bass — the swing comes from the fingers, not a drummer.
This performance comes from her Live in Paris concert, filmed at the Olympia Theatre in December 2001.
The Live in Paris album went on to win Krall the Grammy for Best Jazz Vocal Album.
Nat King Cole's trio made this lean format famous in the '40s — piano out front, guitar and bass keeping the bounce.
All for You earned the young Krall her very first Grammy nomination.
Krall always introduces herself as a pianist first — the singing, she insists, came second.
Hear how she leaves space between phrases? That's the Nat King Cole Trio school of cool, faithfully attended.
Elvis Costello was a big fan of her playing. He later became her husband — they married in 2003.

title: What's Going On
description: Marvin's gentle, devastating question to America — the single Berry Gordy nearly refused to release, from the album Rolling Stone later named the greatest of all time.

pops.text: It began with Renaldo 'Obie' Benson of the Four Tops watching police beat anti-war protesters in Berkeley in 1969.
Benson brought the idea to Al Cleveland and Marvin, who shaped it into a returning Vietnam vet's story — thinking of his brother Frankie, who'd served.
That's saxophonist Eli Fontaine just warming up — he thought he was goofing around. Marvin told him that WAS the take.
Motown boss Berry Gordy reportedly called it the worst record he'd ever heard. Too political, too jazzy, too different.
Marvin refused to record anything else until Gordy released it. The standoff worked — the single soared to #2 pop and #1 R&B.
Hear the party chatter underneath? That's friends and Detroit Lions players Mel Farr and Lem Barney, captured at a studio get-together.
Session legend says bassist James Jamerson, fresh from a night out, played that famous bass line lying flat on his back.
Gordy then demanded a whole album — fast. Marvin delivered the entire What's Going On LP in about a month.
This official video arrived in 2019 — 48 years after the song — filmed in Detroit and Flint, Michigan.
In 2020, Rolling Stone ranked What's Going On #1 on its list of the 500 greatest albums of all time.

title: Superstition
description: Stevie's unstoppable clavinet-funk warning against believing in bad omens — a #1 hit written almost by accident during a jam session with Jeff Beck.

pops.text: That impossibly funky keyboard is a Hohner Clavinet — Stevie basically turned it into a second electric guitar.
The opening drum groove came from Jeff Beck during a jam. Stevie told him to keep playing and improvised the riff on the spot.
Stevie actually wrote this one FOR Beck — but Beck's version got delayed, Motown rushed Stevie's out first, and it hit #1.
Stevie played nearly everything himself — drums, clavinet, synth bass — at just 22 years old.
Engineers Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff conjured the synth sounds from their giant system, nicknamed TONTO.
Stevie had just renegotiated his Motown contract at 21, winning total creative control — almost unheard of at the time.
It's from Talking Book, named because Stevie thought of the songs as chapters. The cover is a rare photo of him without sunglasses.
The lyric is a sermon against superstition itself — broken mirrors, ladders, the number 13. Don't let fear drive.
Stevie performed this live on Sesame Street in 1973 — possibly the funkiest five minutes in children's TV history.
'Superstition' topped the Hot 100 in January 1973 and was later inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.

title: My Girl
description: Smokey Robinson wrote it for David Ruffin's voice, and it became the Temptations' first #1 — quite possibly the most beloved bass intro in pop history.

pops.text: That opening bass line is James Jamerson — Motown's Funk Brothers quietly powering yet another classic.
Then comes Robert White's guitar figure — a handful of notes that everybody on Earth can hum.
Smokey Robinson and fellow Miracle Ronnie White wrote it as a companion piece to Smokey's Mary Wells hit 'My Guy.'
Smokey had one singer in mind: David Ruffin, whom he called the group's 'sleeping giant.' He wrote it to Ruffin's voice.
They cut it at Hitsville U.S.A.'s Studio A — the 'Snakepit,' a converted garage at 2648 West Grand Boulevard in Detroit.
Released just before Christmas 1964, it climbed to #1 on the Billboard Hot 100 by March 1965 — the Temps' first chart-topper.
Ruffin's signature glasses were part style, part necessity — and his look out front became the group's visual trademark.
The song entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1998 and joined the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry in 2017.
Smokey first played it for Ruffin at a piano backstage at the Apollo Theatre in New York. Ruffin loved it instantly.
Audiences once booed when the Temptations tried leaving it out of a show. It has closed the argument ever since.

title: I Want You Back
description: The Jackson 5's debut Motown single — an 11-year-old Michael Jackson announcing himself over the happiest bass line ever recorded.

pops.text: Before Michael sings a note: that piano glissando and Wilton Felder's bouncing bass line. Pop perfection in ten seconds.
This began life as 'I Wanna Be Free,' written for Gladys Knight & the Pips — then Berry Gordy had it rebuilt for his new kid group.
The writers were a Motown hit squad called The Corporation: Gordy, Freddie Perren, Fonce Mizell and Deke Richards.
Michael Jackson was 11 years old. Eleven! And he sang lead like he'd been doing it for decades.
It was recorded in Los Angeles with top session players — reportedly the most expensive single Motown had ever made at that point.
Released in October 1969, it hit #1 on the Hot 100 on January 31, 1970, and ruled the R&B chart for four weeks.
The debut album says 'Diana Ross Presents' — but singer Bobby Taylor actually brought the brothers to Motown, with Gladys Knight cheering them on.
It kicked off four straight #1 singles — this, 'ABC,' 'The Love You Save' and 'I'll Be There.' A debut run like no other.
That bass line later powered Jay-Z's 'Izzo (H.O.V.A.)' in 2001, produced by a young Kanye West.
A new generation met it over the end credits of Guardians of the Galaxy (2014). Baby Groot approved.

title: Three Little Birds
description: Reggae's ultimate reassurance, from the Exodus album — reborn in a 2020 animated video where the Big Bad Wolf learns to chill.

pops.text: Two origin stories compete. Friend Tony Gilbert swears three canaries used to perch outside Bob's window at 56 Hope Road in Kingston.
The other story: 'three little birds' was Bob's pet name for the I Threes — his backing singers, including his wife Rita.
It's from Exodus (1977) — the album Time magazine later named the best album of the entire 20th century.
Marley recorded Exodus in London, living in exile after surviving an attempt on his life in Jamaica in December 1976.
It wasn't released as a single until 1980 — three years after the album — and still reached #17 in the UK.
Half the world thinks the title is 'Don't Worry About a Thing.' It isn't — but as choruses go, that's immortality.
This animated video arrived in 2020 for Marley75, the year-long celebration of what would have been Bob's 75th birthday.
The cartoon flips the Three Little Pigs story — the pig wins the wolf over with kindness and a shared picnic instead of bricks.
Bob's daughter Cedella said the song 'has helped provide hope and light for so many over the years, including me.'
The video has passed 240 million views. The little birds are still singing on doorsteps everywhere.

title: No Woman, No Cry
description: The beloved version isn't the studio take — it's this live recording from London's Lyceum Theatre in 1975, a Trenchtown lullaby for hard times, paired with a 2020 video split between Jamaica and New York.

pops.text: First, the translation: in Jamaican patois it's 'No, woman, nuh cry' — don't cry. It's a comfort, not a complaint.
A studio version appeared on Natty Dread (1974), but this slower Lyceum Theatre performance from July 1975 became the definitive one.
Marley credited the song to Vincent Ford, his childhood friend who ran a soup kitchen in Trenchtown — the royalties helped keep people fed.
The 'government yard in Trenchtown' is real — Marley grew up in Kingston's government housing, cooking cornmeal porridge over logwood fires.
That's Aston 'Family Man' Barrett on bass and his brother Carlton on drums — the Wailers' heartbeat.
The I Threes — Rita Marley, Marcia Griffiths and Judy Mowatt — wrap the chorus in sisterly harmony.
The live single reached #22 in the UK in 1975; reissued after Marley's death in 1981, it climbed to #8.
This 2020 video splits the story between a mother holding things together in Jamaica and a father driving a cab in New York.
The Fugees' 1996 cover carried the song to a whole hip-hop generation.
Rolling Stone placed it among the 500 greatest songs of all time — Trenchtown's porridge pot is now music history.

title: I Can See Clearly Now
description: Cliff's sunshine-soaked cover of Johnny Nash's classic, recorded for Cool Runnings — the Jamaican bobsled movie — and the biggest American hit of his long career.

pops.text: Johnny Nash wrote it, and his original topped the US chart for four weeks back in 1972.
Nash cut his version in London with Jamaican session band the Fabulous Five — reggae was already traveling the world.
Cliff recorded his take for Cool Runnings (1993), the comedy about Jamaica's first Olympic bobsled team.
The film is loosely true — Jamaica really did debut a bobsled team at the 1988 Calgary Winter Olympics.
This became Cliff's highest-charting US single ever — #18 on the Hot 100, a quarter-century after his previous American hit.
It went all the way to #1 in France, Iceland and New Zealand. The whole planet needed the sunshine.
Cliff — born James Chambers — was a star before Bob Marley went global; Jamaica sent him to the 1964 World's Fair as a teen representative.
He also starred in The Harder They Come (1972), the film that carried reggae to the wider world.
The video was directed by Scott Hamilton Kennedy, who later earned an Academy Award nomination as a documentary filmmaker.
Cliff was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2010. The sunshine is fully earned.
